segments.text: Hey friends, have you
ever asked yourself this question—why do bad habits feel so good?
Like eating junk food, pani puri,
burgers, pizza—ohhhoo, sweet things—just thinking about them makes my mouth water.
There are also other bad habits, like scrolling on your phone
all day, wasting time, watching porn, watching inappropriate things,
doing inappropriate things, or other types of addictions.
Once you do it, you feel like doing it again and again.
We know these are bad habits and shouldn’t be a part of our life.
Yet, they easily creep into our lives, and we keep repeating them.
On the other hand, good habits are really beneficial.
We know this, but still, we struggle to bring them into our lives. Why?
Well, the author of Atomic Habits, James
Clear, gives an answer to this in his book.
I’m going to explain this to you in great detail today.
Specifically, there
are four characteristics that we usually apply a lot to bad habits.
Because of these, even bad habits start feeling good to us.
On the other hand, good habits lack these
four characteristics, which is why we struggle to bring them into our lives.
If you look
at page number 212 of this book, you’ll find the crux of the entire book there.
And that’s exactly what I’m going to explain to you today.
I’ll tell you about the four characteristics—Make
it Obvious, Make it Attractive, Make it Easy, and Make it Satisfying—and how
you should apply them to good habits.
At the same time, you need to reverse them for bad habits.
Only then will bad habits leave your life, and good habits will take their place.
Because, as we all know, our life is nothing but a product—a product of what?
A product of all the actions we take regularly, which means our habits.
And if we develop good habits, our life will change—whether it’s in terms
of health, wealth, relationships, or happiness.
That’s why today’s video is going to be one of the best videos for your life!
I guarantee you the best summary of Atomic Habits!
I’m going to explain the entire table to you—how you need to apply four key
things to good habits so that they stick and don’t just come and go.
At the same time, you’ll need to reverse these four
things for bad habits so that they disappear from your life.
This is the entire table, and I’m going to explain it to you very easily.
Plus, I’ll show you how
you can apply all these principles in your life with just one simple action.
I’ll also share what I’m personally doing and encourage you to do the same.
Stay tuned to learn more!
Now, let’s start! The first characteristic that makes bad
habits so tempting is “Make it Obvious.” How many of you
watching this video have a habit of eating something sweet after a meal?
You must have noticed this—even when a friend or relative has eaten so much that
their stomach is completely full, there’s absolutely no space
left for more food, yet they still crave something sweet!
Their stomach is so tight that
at any moment, a shirt button could fly off and hit someone in the eye!
But still, if you ask that person, “Are you full?” they’ll say, “Yes.” But
if you
ask, “Will you have something sweet?” they’ll reply, “Oh, there’s
always room for dessert!”—and they’ll eat sweets wholeheartedly.
This action clearly shows how powerful this bad habit is. Why is
it so powerful? Because this habit is very obvious!
The culture we live in has made eating something sweet after a meal so common,
so obvious that if you don’t do it, it feels strange.
That’s why, many times, when you go to a restaurant—you enjoy your meal, order
starters, and the main course—but if you don’t order dessert, even the waiter will.
Even the waiter will judge you, thinking, “Why aren’t they ordering dessert?”—and
you will also feel like something
is missing. Well, when something is made this obvious, like “At this time,
you must do this thing,” it becomes very easy for that habit
to become permanent. And you’ll see this happening a lot with bad habits!
For example, the moment you feel bored, what’s the obvious
solution? Use the internet, waste time. Feeling lazy?
The obvious
go-to action is to quickly grab your phone, use the internet, scroll through
social media. You have a clear, obvious path—you know exactly how to waste your
time. But on the other hand, healthy habits don’t work this way.
You must have noticed—these days, there are so many videos about what’s healthy
and what’s not. If you want to eat a salad, there are so many types of salads.
Which one should you eat?
When should you eat it? Some say eat it in between meals, some say eat it first,
others say drink milk, while some say milk
is bad. This happens with good habits—you’ll
notice that nothing is obvious; instead, everything is confusing.
Some people say this food is good, while others say, no, even this food isn’t
good. So, what does our brain do? It says, “Forget it!
Both of these foods are confusing.” And then it goes straight for junk food,
because that’s something we obviously know we enjoy. The same thing
happens with watching TV—pay attention to when this habit develops.
Usually, people watch
TV while eating—including me, I’m guilty of this too! Why does this happen?
Because it’s obvious. We already know that
as soon as we sit down to eat, we should turn on the TV. Even in relationships,
bad habits often become
very obvious. If you feel even a little naughty, there’s already an obvious
answer in your mind—you know exactly which website to open,
where to go, and what to do. There’s already a clearly defined path for it!
Whenever something makes us feel naughty or gives us a sense of self-love,
we already have a defined path in our minds—and we simply follow it. In other
words, it’s obvious.
The same thing applies to happiness—many addictive things are also very obvious.
For example, “If I meet this friend, I’ll do this specific thing
with them.” “I’ll do this bad habit, and it will make me happy.
I’ll enjoy it.” But when
it comes to good habits, things aren’t that obvious. Want to eat a salad?
What should be in the salad?
No idea. How to make it tasty?
No idea. When to eat it? How to eat it?
How much to eat?—So much confusion! The same goes for many other
health-related food choices—they come with a lot of confusion.
Since it’s not obvious, it creates
confusion, and that’s why we don’t do it. Want to go to the gym?
When should you go? Some say morning, others say evening—again,
confusion. So, what does the brain say? “Forget it, bro!
Just stay where you are.” Now, if you look at relationships,
what’s a good habit? Building confidence. Going up and
talking to your ideal partner. But even here, your mind is full of confusion.
“When should I talk to them? What should I say?
What shouldn’t I say?” Again, you don’t have an obvious path, so what happens?
You don’t do it. Instead, you go back to scrolling on your phone, stalking
some attractive girl, and doing whatever comes next. But when it comes
to happiness and spirituality, we all know we should be more spiritual.
Many people watching this video might be very religious, but again, there’s
confusion in this too. Some people say,
“Do this.” Others say, “No, you shouldn’t do this.
It’s against our religion.” So, what happens? You end up with
so much confusion that you don’t even know exactly what to do—and because of that.
You won’t adopt good habits in your life. To make things obvious, you can
do three things: 1.
Implementation Intention Whatever good habit
you want to bring into your life, decide clearly: When will you do it? Where
will you do it? What exactly is the habit? If you clearly define these
things, your intention to implement the habit will
be set. This will increase the probability of making it obvious and
actually doing it!
So, do this! 2.
Habit Stacking This means attaching your new habit to an existing habit you
already do. For example, here’s what I did: I made it a rule to eat salad
before meals. Eating salad is a good habit, so what did I do? I started
doing it right before my meal—linking it to something I already do every day!
Because of this, I naturally developed the habit of eating
salad before every meal. On the other hand, watching TV while eating
is a bad habit that has stuck with me because
of habit stacking—and that’s something I want to remove from my life.
So, you see, the formula is the same. If we use it for a good habit,
it will work. If we use it for a bad habit, that will also become a habit!
And what’s the 3rd thing? Creating a Good Environment If you feel hungry
often and eat too
much junk food, then what should you do? Make those junk foods invisible!
Keep them away. Instead of keeping
junk food near your bed, put it somewhere far away, in a corner where
you can’t see it. Similarly, if you want to develop a good habit, do the same!
So, set up your environment in a way that makes it easy for you to do that thing.
For example, if you want to read books, keep more books around you.
So that whenever you see them, you get a signal like, “Okay, I have to read a
book.” And then, you actually read it. Similarly,
by following these three things, you can make your good habits
obvious and eliminate bad habits by making them invisible.
Keep it away from your sight and environment. Make it
as confusing as possible, don’t bring clarity to it, and don’t set a clear path
for it. Now, the next characteristic is: Make it Attractive vs.
Make it Unattractive I want you to close your eyes and think about your
favorite junk food—
that unhealthy food that you absolutely love eating and enjoy the most.
As soon as you think about it for a while, I am so sure that your mouth
might start watering. Why?
Because food is very attractive to you. Have you ever noticed
how junk food advertisements are made? They are designed
to be highly attractive. Take Coca-Cola ads, for example. What is it really?
Just black sugary water. But the way they present it—it
looks so appealing that it feels like an amazing and irresistible thing.
They have made it so attractive that what happens? Many times, when
we feel thirsty and go to eat or drink something, we end up ordering cola
or similar drinks instead of water. Because it is very attractive.
Similarly, junk food also looks very attractive to us. But
on the other hand, if you look at salad, it doesn’t appear that attractive.
Normal vegetables, if you look at them, don’t appear that attractive.
Going to the gym often doesn’t feel very attractive. When it comes
to wealth, spending money on new things feels very attractive. Buying new
clothes and showing them to others—what
does this do? It feels attractive to us and also attracts others
toward us. That’s why people develop a habit of constantly buying new things.
We can’t afford an iPhone, yet we buy it on EMI. Why? Because
it’s attractive, it feels exciting. Spending money seems like an attractive
feature, while earning
money? Nobody notices that—it doesn’t feel as attractive. Working hard,
getting scolded, hustling day and night without worrying
about things—these things don’t look or feel attractive. That’s why we
don’t enjoy putting in hard work and doing all these things.
Whereas buying things or going to a Coldplay concert feels very attractive
to us. From a relationship perspective, look at how much Instagram and similar
platforms are being used today.
Why? Because they are filled with attractive things. We all
know that God made women beautiful and made men powerful and
strong. And what does Instagram do? It amplifies that attractiveness by 10x.
How? Girls are already naturally attractive, but nowadays, what
do they do? They get surgeries, apply makeup, use filters, and then pose
in ways that make them look even more attractive. And
because of this, most guys end up mindlessly scrolling on Instagram,
getting trapped in bad habits, and spending too much time on the internet.
Whereas, on the other hand, real people in real relationships often don’t seem
as attractive. They don’t have the 5x or 10x power of filters, surgeries,
or makeup. And because of this, sometimes even good people—modest and
genuinely kind-hearted girls who could be great for you—don’t seem as appealing.
There is no attraction towards them. People stay glued to their phones and fail
to build meaningful relationships. And even if a girl is attractive, at the
very least, we should find it appealing to go and talk to her, to build confidence,
to discuss difficult situations, or even to talk to our parents. But these
things don’t seem attractive, which is why they never become habits in our lives.
When it comes to happiness, notice this— In movies these days, you will always
see the hero smoking a cigarette, looking extremely
cool and attractive. Because of this, from a young age, we start feeling
like we also want to be heroes. And to become a hero, what do we do?
We start smoking too. Smoking, drinking
alcohol—all these things are marketed in a very attractive way.
Directly or indirectly, it is repeatedly shown that all these bad habits are very
attractive. Because of this, we naturally get attracted to them—it’s
as simple as that. On the other hand, good habits—like drinking plain
water, going for
a walk, or talking to your family—don’t seem attractive to us. Why?
Because no money is being spent on marketing them.
Now, this again becomes a problem.
What’s the solution? How can we make good habits more attractive?
Well, again, I’ll tell you three things. First: Use Temptation Building
Whatever good habit you want to build in your life—for example, waking
up early in the morning—attach it to a temptation. For example:
If you want to wake up early, pair it with something tempting.
For example, if you love drinking coffee, tea, or juice, and you
know it’s good for your health, then link that habit with waking up early.
Tell yourself: “As soon as I wake up, I’ll drink my coffee while doing
my work.” What is Temptation Building? It’s simple—connect something you want
to do with something you need to do. The Second Thing
To make a habit more attractive, join a culture that supports it.
Join people where the habit you want to build is completely normal.
For example, if you want to develop the habit of going to the gym
or waking up early, become part of a group where everyone wakes up early. Why?
Because humans are
social creatures—we tend to follow what others around us are doing.
If many people around you are waking up early,
you will feel more motivated to wake up early too.
But if you keep watching videos
saying, “I’m a night owl, I don’t like waking up early, I’m
so cool,” then what will happen? You’ll start thinking, “I want to
be cool too, I’ll also stay up late.” And since this
is easy to do and enjoyable, you’ll naturally fall into that habit.
Instead of celebrating the wrong habits, celebrate the good habits.
Surround yourself with people who have already built the positive habit you want
to develop in your life. Next, to make things more attractive, create rituals.
For example, if you observe, many people have daily rituals—waking up, brushing
their teeth, going to the toilet, maybe praying, and then eating a good meal.
In this, the author basically says that before doing any good habit you want
to develop in your life, create a ritual by doing something you really enjoy.
For example, eating a piece of dark chocolate, listening
to motivational music, or doing anything that excites you.
This way, you create a ritual linked to the good habit, making it easier
to follow.
On the other hand, you need to do the exact opposite
to remove a bad habit from your life. What should you do?
Make it as unattractive as possible. Remember
this: Watch videos that show how harmful and uncool smoking actually is. For any
bad habit you have in your life, visualize its negative effects, listen to people
talking about its downsides, and make it as unappealing as possible in your mind.
The more unattractive it becomes to you, the higher the chances that the habit
will fade from your life. For both breaking
bad habits and building good habits, you need to focus on: Make it easy vs.
Make it difficult. Notice how easy it has become to eat unhealthy food
today. No matter where you go, the moment you step outside, junk food
is readily available.
You will easily find a shop on every street corner selling sweet and
tasty food that is cheap but unhealthy for you. On the other hand, if you go out
looking for something healthy, it will
be expensive and harder to find. For example, I live in Mumbai.
There is a place called Kurla, and right next to it is my office mall, Phoenix
Mall. If I feel like eating something there, healthy options are very limited,
and even if they are available, they are very expensive and not as enjoyable.
Whenever I think of a healthy option, the
only thing that comes to my mind is Subway, to some extent.
Even that, as you know, is not really that healthy. But if I think about
unhealthy options, the entire food court is filled with them—they are cheaper,
tastier, and more enjoyable. Not just in terms of food, but if you look
at relationships as well, self-love has become very easy, just like I
am explaining to you.
Masturbation, watching porn—all of this is very easy. You can do
it quickly, without
spending any money or investing much time. It’s very easy
to engage in the wrong things, and you’ll even enjoy it—everything will seem
fine. But on the other hand, getting into a meaningful,
real relationship, talking to a
real girl whom you actually like—that’s a different challenge altogether.
The girl with whom you may want to build a long-term relationship in the future,
maybe even marry—talking to her, building a good relationship
with her—that’s difficult. That’s why our mind gravitates toward
the easier option and pushes us to do what is effortless. Similarly, when
it comes to wealth, just staying at home and doing nothing is very easy.
Doing nothing and just scrolling on your mobile is very easy. But if I
tell you to go and learn a skill to make money, develop
talent within yourself, bring discipline into your life—that’s difficult. If I
ask you to read a book, it feels even more difficult, right?
No matter how much I explain, you won’t feel like doing it because it’s hard.
And if you observe closely, in any situation where you have an easy option
and a difficult option, we always tend to choose the easy one.
We always choose the easy habit. Notice this even in terms of happiness.
Some time ago, I went to Rajasthan for a podcast with Rahul Malodia Ji.
While I was on
my way there, unfortunately, I forgot to bring a book
from the airport. So, I was looking around on my way from the airport to their
office, thinking about getting a book for him.
A book would have been a great
gift for him. But I kept searching and searching, and guess what?
Not a single bookstore was visible on my way. Whereas, on the
other hand, cigarette shops and even liquor stores were everywhere.
I could spot one on almost every street. This clearly shows how easy
it is—if you want to feel happy, you can get it so easily.
You can easily achieve happiness by becoming an addict, consuming
substances, and getting high. But if you want to achieve happiness through
reading books, developing good habits, or spirituality, it has been made
so difficult in today’s society. So, what’s the solution? Well, the solution
is to start making bad habits difficult and start making good habits easier.
For this, what should you do? Well, in this book, the author shares
many techniques, and I will share some of them with you. One key technique is
to reduce the number of steps required to build a good habit. For example,
if you want to develop the habit of going to the gym, but every morning you have
to wake up, find your workout clothes, and go through a lot of hassle,
it becomes difficult.
After that, you will pack your gym bag, wear your shoes, and then go to the gym.
This involves too many steps, making it difficult. So, what should you do?
Make it easy. Maybe prepare your gym bag before going to bed. Or sleep
in the clothes you plan to wear to the gym. What will this do?
Things will become easier. You will only need to take one step—maybe wake
up in the morning or in the afternoon, pick up your bag, and just head to the
gym. The more you simplify the steps, the easier it will be to build that habit
in your life. On the other hand, the more steps you
add between yourself and a bad habit, the less you will feel like doing it.
For example, if you have a strong craving for sweets, and you keep them within
arm’s reach, where you just have to pick them up and eat, then it’s easy, and you
will keep eating them repeatedly. But if you put those sweets in a box, then put
that box inside another box, and then inside yet another
box, making it harder to access—just think about it yourself.
If you crave sweets, will you really go and open box after box every time?
You might do it occasionally, but the probability will be very low, and the
chance of repeating it frequently will be even lower. So, the first thing you
should do is: For good habits, reduce the number of steps required.
For bad habits, increase the number of steps, which is called friction.
Then, you can use the 2-minute rule. Basically, whenever you want to build a
good habit, you often overcommit by making big promises,
like: “If I go to the gym, I’ll do this, I’ll do that...
I’ll work out for an hour and complete all exercises.”
Don’t think like that. Just tell yourself: “I’ll go to the
gym for just 2 minutes and do whatever exercise I need to for 2 minutes.”
When you start trying
to do any good habit for just 2 minutes, you’ll notice that the biggest
friction is simply getting started. Once that initial resistance is broken,
you’ll automatically feel like doing more.
In fact, the author even says that it’s
okay not to do it for half an hour—even if you stop after 2 minutes, it’s fine!
Just go for 2 minutes. The author gives an example of a guy who used to go
to the gym just for 2 minutes, check the place, and then leave. He did this for
a month, and once he built the habit of going, he naturally started working
out and eventually transformed his body. Similarly, follow the 2-minute rule!
If you want to read books, don’t think about finishing the whole book. Just
think, I will read for 2 minutes, and read for 2 minutes. Once the habit
is built, then improve it and increase the duration. Next, what you can do
is automate your habit. Buy a subscription or set up something
that allows you to take action once and then repeat it automatically.
If you love reading books, then maybe buy a subscription related to it,
so that books keep coming
to you. When you constantly have new books arriving, you will at least read one
page again and again. This will slowly make you realize that you are a reader,
and you will naturally start reading more.
If you want to go to the gym, then get a subscription for it.
Make a commitment with a friend, like saying, “We
will definitely go to the gym together, and if I don’t go, you can
keep this amount of my money.” If you set such a commitment, the chances of you
going to the gym will increase. Another method is called “Master the Decisive
Moment.” How good
or bad your life turns out is defined by the decisions you make. For
example, if you chose to watch this video, that itself is a positive decision.
Similarly, whenever you get a chance to make a decision, choose the one that
takes you closer to your ideal self, the best version of yourself.
For example, watching a video and taking action. Even after watching this
video, you will have a decision to make— Should you take action on what you
learned, or just close this video and watch something else? Should you waste
time scrolling, or just go to sleep? These decisive moments
keep coming, and what you choose in those moments shapes your future.
Start mastering those decisive moments. All these strategies will make it easier
to build good habits in your life. And if you do the opposite, your bad habits
will start fading away. In the “Make It Difficult” approach, the author
mentions two key things: Increase the number of steps (to make bad
habits harder). Use the technique I mentioned earlier (friction and barriers).
You can create commitment devices. Maybe make a public commitment—comment
on social media saying, “I am taking a 21-day challenge” or “I will go
to the gym daily from now on.” By doing this, if you
don’t follow through, it will create a problem for you (social pressure).
If there’s a penalty, we often don’t like to look bad or waste our money.
So, when you make a commitment—whether through your words, time,
or money—it becomes difficult to back out. Especially if you’ve
invested a significant amount of money, it adds more pressure to follow through.
And now, since we’re talking about 21 days, you probably already know.
All the concepts from Atomic Habits are something we are actively applying in our
own lives. That means I myself am following them, along with many others
who are already participating in the 21-day challenge with me.
In this challenge, we committed to learning something
positive every morning, practicing meditation, visualization, affirmations,
and engaging in activities that boost our self-confidence—along with many other
interesting habits.
We continuously learn and take action on topics related to health, wealth,
relationships, and happiness in the 21-day challenge, all based on the principles
of Atomic Habits. If you’re interested, make sure to watch the video till the
end, as I’ll be sharing details on how you can join the 21-day challenge. Now,
let’s move on to the fourth and final characteristic—which
is something you must implement if you want to build good habits.
Imagine this scenario: You are extremely hungry. Now, you have two options:
The first option is that there is a junk food shop right next to you, offering
cheap, tasty food that will quickly satisfy your hunger. The second option
is to resist the temptation, go home, cook food or have it prepared,
and then eat a healthy salad.
Look at both options carefully.
The second option might take a lot of time, and maybe by the time you’re
done, your hunger might even go away. Now tell me, which option
feels more satisfying? Obviously, the junk food option feels more satisfying.
Why? Because it’s quick, it fills your stomach fast, and
you feel satisfied instantly. And this is exactly what happens most of the time.
In life, when it comes to wealth, just thinking about wealth or blaming
others feels very satisfying. Saying things like: “The government is bad.”
“The world is unfair.” “Life is tough.” “People are the reason I’m
not successful.” Blaming others feels satisfying because it makes us believe
it’s not our fault. But I once heard a quote.
“If you want to feel good, blame others.
But if you want to get better, take responsibility.”
Blaming others feels satisfying—it’s easy to do, and our brain naturally prefers
it. On the other hand, holding yourself accountable isn’t always easy.
It’s uncomfortable, but that’s where real growth happens. Recently, I was
learning two important skills related
to wealth building, and they don’t always feel instantly satisfying.
Bad habits feel very satisfying.
Even if you’re feeling slightly uncomfortable,
using your phone instantly gives you satisfaction—a quick dopamine
hit. But when we build good habits, the satisfaction is delayed.
You do feel satisfied, but only after some effort and time. That’s
why, when faced with two options—instant satisfaction or delayed
satisfaction—we often choose instant
gratification. This applies to health, wealth, and relationships as well.
If you think about it, why do people engage in masturbation?
Instant gratification is the key. Why do people do drugs for happiness?
Because it gives instant pleasure—it makes
them feel great right away. The same happiness can be achieved through
prayer, meditation, or connecting with a higher power, but it takes time.
The satisfaction is delayed. That’s why
people avoid these long-term rewarding habits and
instead choose instant pleasures—which is exactly what we shouldn’t be doing.
So, the solution to this problem is simple: Make good habits as satisfying
as possible and make bad habits as unsatisfying
as possible. How can you do this?
Here are three strategies from this book: Use Reinforcement –
Whenever you do something good, immediately reward yourself.
What do we usually do to ourselves?
Whenever we do something good—like if someone wants to become a content
writer and they create a video—they should reward themselves.
But instead of rewarding themselves, they start punishing themselves.
They think, “Oh, I didn’t make a good video,” “The quality wasn’t great,”
“I didn’t speak well.” But instead of giving a reward, what do they do?
I made a video, and instead of rewarding myself, I started punishing myself.
But isn’t punishment what makes bad habits feel satisfying? We don’t judge
ourselves as much for bad habits, but whenever
we do something good, we judge ourselves harshly.
We overanalyze and make it unsatisfying.
That’s completely wrong! Do the opposite—reward yourself.
Give yourself a treat, do something
that makes you feel good, something that feels like a reward in your own way.
91 symbols, like chocolates, that aren’t overly unhealthy but rather healthy.
The second thing you can do to make habits satisfying is habit tracking. For
example, when we
do an Independence Challenge, we create a habit tracking system where we mark
an “X” every day to track progress—one day done, two days done.
When you see your streak continuing, it feels really good and motivating!
It gives a satisfying feeling that yes, I am working consistently on myself and
my goals. You can also start habit tracking like this. One more thing
you can do is never skip twice. When you track your habits, there might
be a day when you tried your best, but you fell sick or something happened at home.
If you miss a habit for some reason, always remember
this rule: Never miss two days in a row. Because once you start skipping
one or two days, missing the third day becomes easier, then
the fourth day, and soon your habit will completely break. That’s why it’s
better to track your habits and never skip twice. If you follow all
these things, you will feel a lot more satisfaction and progress.
You will feel proud of yourself.
You will experience the winner’s effect, which will further strengthen
your good habits. On the other hand, you can do the opposite for bad habits.
Get an accountability partner—someone who reminds you repeatedly
that a habit is bad and stops you from doing it. This will make it harder
to feel satisfied with bad habits. What we should create is a system where
we appreciate progress and hold ourselves accountable.
But if someone keeps telling
you repeatedly that what you’re doing is wrong, how will you feel?
Unsatisfied. So, try to have an accountability partner.
Create a habit contract for yourself. How does a contract work?
If it’s broken, there’s a penalty to pay.
Similarly, create a personal
contract where, if you break your habit, you have to pay a price for it.
Still, you should have some form of punishment, so that engaging in a bad
habit feels like a penalty rather than satisfaction.
Be openly honest—combining
all these principles, I have created the Independence Challenge for you.
I want you to observe and apply it. If you truly want to build good habits,
